plate.subject: an ancient king on a hill above his hosts

paragraphs.text: Aen is the legendary founder of Aenor, and he is widely held to be the greatest man who ever lived. He is called the First Man and First of His Name, yet men had lived in great numbers, over many generations, for thousands of years before him. He was born through magic and power, without a direct father. The title speaks of that unique birth and of his place as founder of the united realm of men. It does not mean that he was the first man to live.

sources.section: The Ainu and the First Men

paragraphs.text: The men of that far older world were stronger, more gifted in magic and far longer-lived than the men of later ages. Some of them held a power like that of gods without being gods. Aen himself lived an extraordinarily long life and fathered hundreds of sons. His blood is held to be the most royal of all mankind.

sources.section: The Ainu and the First Men

paragraphs.text: Aen fought in the War of Men for hundreds of years and united the rival kingdoms of men into a single kingdom. The War of Men was fought before the First Age; his victory and the founding of Aenor mark Year 1 of the First Age, which lasted 1,675 years. His victory brought centuries of peace to the central realm of men, although the later spread of that realm to distant frontiers stayed violent.
Aen is remembered dark-haired and bearded, with a very powerful presence. He is shown crowned, in a black and red cloak.

No chronicle tells where Aen first appeared, or what power brought about his birth. It is not known when he died, or who ruled after him. The scholars do not agree whether the name Ainu means all the mighty men of the early world, Aen’s house alone, or a people older than both, nor whether Aenor was named in his honour.

entries.title: Ein, Son of Aen
entries.subtitle: First Age · Royal Line of Aen

paragraphs.text: Ein is a son of Aen, the first king and unifier of men. Aen fathered hundreds of sons and left many descendants, whose lines became rival branches of the royal house. Ein’s line is counted the most direct of them all.

Little of Ein himself is written. No chronicle tells of his reign, of his death, of the mother of his children, or of his place among the early kings of Aenor. In later ages his line was held to be lost, and why, no chronicle tells.
Ein is the father of Eindil, the Man from the Ice. Eindil is son of Ein, son of Aen, and of the royal blood that stands closest to the founder’s own.

Ein had another son, Afrit, born in about the same years as Eindil. Ein refused Afrit the royal succession. After Afrit betrayed his brother, the disappointed prince turned slowly toward corruption and demonic power. Why Ein refused him, how Afrit betrayed Eindil, and which of the two brothers is the elder, no chronicle tells.

plate.subject: a cloaked figure on a snow ridge, from behind

paragraphs.text: In the late Fourth Age a man was found alive in the ice of the Cold Lands, and the local tribes who found him took him in. He did not remember his name, his people or where he came from. His strength was extraordinary, beyond that of any man they knew, and he was unwilling to misuse it. He has black hair and blue eyes that glow faintly. No chronicle tells how he came to lie in the ice, or for how long.
paragraphs.note: “unwilling to misuse it” follows the chronicle outline, not a vault sentence

paragraphs.text: Travellers of the West Lands took the stranger south. He aided their communities, made peace between rivals and for a short time served as a western king. Sailing for Aenor, he was driven by storm to the Islands of the South, and from there he went on to the Lands of the Sun, where Lorien, King of the Gala, spoke with him and sent him north.

He sailed north toward the Castle of Yeldenne. Every companion of that voyage died in an ambush, and the stranger went on alone through the snow to the castle. There Horos, dying, gave him Glo, a crystal of old and holy power, and his blue sword.

At Gala, Lorien named him: Eindil, son of Ein, son of Aen. He comes of the First Men, whose gifts of magic, long life and strength were greater than those of later men. He is the strongest man remembered in the Fourth Age, and of the royal blood closest to the founder’s line. He had been held in a sleep of many ages, by means no chronicle tells.

Eindil is the brother of Afrit, the Deliverer worshipped in Aenor; both are sons of Ein, born in about the same years. At Yeldenne Eindil learned that the god-king of Aenor was his brother. Which of the two is the elder, no chronicle tells.
In the War of the Last Crowns Volgan struck Eindil down. The New Gods revived him and gave him extraordinary power through Glo. Whether the powers the gods gave him are his for ever is not known.
Afrit returned, struck Eindil, cut off one of his arms and cast him from a cliff. Eindil survived the fall.

In the royal palace Eindil took on his brother, with Alleria of Selen and Golbran at his side. They stripped away the artifacts that sustained Afrit, and Eindil killed him. Golbran gave his life to preserve Eindil.
Eindil took the Necklace of the Abyss and wears it. What it will do to him, no chronicle tells.
Eindil returned to the royal palace and was crowned King of Aenor, and with his crowning the Fourth Age ended.

entries.title: The Deliverer
entries.subtitle: Third and Fourth Ages · The Faith

plate.subject: a sun-disc above a temple door, no face

paragraphs.text: The Deliverer is worshipped across Aoaz as a New God. The temples tell that when Elzon fell at the end of the Third Age, the Deliverer shielded the people from the ruin of his fall and saved them. The people hailed him their Deliverer, the New God of Deliverance, Protection and Renewal, and his worship has grown through the long peace of the Fourth Age.
paragraphs.note: the title “New God of Deliverance, Protection and Renewal” is proposed

sources.section: Afrit in Third and Fourth Age religion

paragraphs.text: Men know him by the name Aurevan. His sacred houses keep granaries, hospitals and the rolls of births, and his priests teach in the schools and counsel the courts and the crown.
paragraphs.note: the name Aurevan and the houses’ granaries, hospitals and birth rolls are proposed; the institutions’ hold on teaching, relief, courts and crown is established

paragraphs.text: He is not one of the twelve main New Gods whom the twelve months honour. His worship keeps a feast in his honour instead of a month.

sources.section: Afrit in Third and Fourth Age religion

paragraphs.text: After the death of the Golden King the Deliverer took Aenor’s crown openly under his public name, Aurevan. He proclaimed himself King of Aenor, First of His Name, and New God of Men, and many worship him as their king.
paragraphs.note: the name Aurevan and the full form of the title are proposed

paragraphs.text: The Deliverer was Afrit, Ein’s son and a grandson of Aen. The name Afrit was known chiefly to his secret council, to his enemies and to certain beings of power. His worship and his powers were real.
Whether he was ever a true New God, of the order the Holy Seven made, is not known. The worship of men cannot by itself prove it.

sources.section: Afrit in Third and Fourth Age religion

entries.title: Afrit
entries.subtitle: All Ages · Prince of the First Men

plate.subject: a cracked golden mask on dark stone

paragraphs.text: Afrit is Ein’s son and a grandson of Aen, born a man of the mighty First Men. His father denied him the throne, and Afrit betrayed his brother. Then he sought dominion through corruption, demonic magic, bargains, worship and artifacts. His demonic form has grown over the ages, but beneath his protections he is still mortal and can be killed.

In the First Age he secretly gathered demons, spirits, men and elves against Volgan, and they helped bring about the dark lord’s defeat at Dardan. He did it to remove a rival and to set himself toward the crown, and nobody saw his hand. In the Second Age he gained worship, networks and supernatural power, and his ascension near its end was one of that age’s defining events. He stayed independent of Elzon and Volgan.

In the Third Age his followers supported the resistance against Elzon, and at Elzon’s fall he helped protect the people’s lives. They hailed him a New God, their Deliverer, and his cult keeps a feast in his honour, not a month. Whether he truly belongs to the order of gods the Holy Seven made is not known. The adoration of men cannot by itself prove it.

sources.section: His later recognition as a New God

paragraphs.text: Through most of the Fourth Age Afrit has governed Aenor from behind the throne, through priests, schools, houses of relief, councillors and kings who are his creatures, and the kingdom has prospered all the while. Ordinary people know him as the Deliverer, by the name Aurevan; his inner council knows him as Afrit. The Golden King is one of the least able kings his hidden rule has steered.
paragraphs.note: the public name Aurevan is proposed

paragraphs.text: He has gathered servants and enchanted artifacts, among them the Ring of Doors. He sent a master thief, Sevrin, into the Abyss for Roka’s Necklace of the Abyss, and he kept his promise of eternal life to him. The necklace greatly increases his strength. Through his council he has built alliances across the East and South Lands, a reserve dominion should Aenor be threatened.
paragraphs.note: the names Ring of Doors and Sevrin are proposed

paragraphs.text: Afrit’s brother is Eindil, the Man from the Ice, who slept through the ages and woke in the Cold Lands. At Yeldenne Horos named Afrit as Eindil’s brother.
Afrit murdered the Golden King and took Aenor’s throne openly under his public name, proclaiming himself King of Men and New God.
In the last war Afrit abandoned Aenor and took a kingship in the east, the King of the East, as the reserve he had long prepared.
Afrit is dead. He died a mortal death, and no chronicle tells of any form of him that survived it.
In the royal palace his brother, helped by Alleria and Golbran, stripped away Afrit’s rings, wards and other artifacts. Golbran tore the Necklace of the Abyss from him, and his brother killed him.

plate.subject: a heavy crowned man under too much gold leaf

paragraphs.text: The Golden King reigns over Aenor in the late Fourth Age. He inherited strong institutions and a flourishing kingdom, and he governs them badly. He is preoccupied with wealth, sells offices and rewards favourites.
He founded the Lost Cause, an order of politics and arms meant to stand against the growing dark powers. He also uses it to raise himself up.
No chronicle gives his personal name, his years or his kin; to all of Aoaz he is the Golden King.
The Golden King died, and with him his reign of gold and favour. His death left Aenor’s crown in dispute.

By his reign the Deliverer, who was Afrit, had spent centuries strengthening his hold on Aenor’s council, clergy and great institutions, and the Golden King had been one of his creatures. Afrit secretly arranged the King’s death and used the crisis that followed to have himself proclaimed king. Few of his worshippers understood it.
A plot against the Golden King’s life was uncovered, and the rising that followed was crushed. The Golden King lives and keeps his crown.

plate.subject: a weary king before many banners

paragraphs.text: Edran was the great king of Aenor who gathered the Grand Alliance and helped defeat Volgan in the late First Age. He is remembered as the greatest king since Aen.

Edran held Aenor together after Dardan and went on guiding its recovery into the early Second Age. He died of disease during the long years of grief and rebuilding. No chronicle names the illness or the year.

His greatest mistake came after Volgan’s banishment. Against strong elven objections he ordered the Grand Alliance to conquer the Ember Lands. Elzon’s defenders inflicted enormous losses and forced the invaders to retreat. The distrust that followed endured for generations: when Elzon later invaded, the elves refused to send armies to help the men of Aenor.
Edran came of a fairly distant line of Aen. His Charter of the Free Banners secured the independence of his allies, among them free realms of the West and of the elves. Men called him the Gatherer.

entries.title: Lorien, King of the Gala
entries.subtitle: All Ages · King of the Gala Elves

paragraphs.text: Lorien is king of the Gala elves of the Lands of the Sun, a being of extraordinary age and power. In the First Age he led the Gala elves in King Edran’s Grand Alliance. He has lived through every age since, and he remembers the War of Men, the defeat of Volgan at Dardan, the fall of Aenor and the reign of Elzon.

Edran’s ruinous attack on the Ember Lands after Dardan brought needless elven deaths and a long estrangement between elves and men. In the Second Age the elves refused to join another war on Aenor’s behalf against Elzon. Yet Lorien still cares for the fate of all Aoaz.
The Gala are the most powerful of the elves, and Lorien looks a figure of myth. His eyes glow an extremely bright yellow, and he wears a robe of white and deep gold.

Late in the Fourth Age Lorien welcomed a stranger from the Islands of the South and spoke with him over many weeks. He named him Eindil, son of Ein, grandson of Aen, and told him of Aoaz long before Aen. Through a vision in the Mirror of First Rain he warned of a catastrophe drawing near.
paragraphs.note: the Mirror of First Rain is proposed

paragraphs.text: Lorien sent Eindil to Horos at Yeldenne to obtain Glo. He gave him a remarkable ship, armour, a sword and companions from many peoples: western friends, southern islanders and Gala elves.

When Kusven came forth out of the black north at the end of the Fourth Age, Lorien returned with ancient lords and spirits to defend all the living peoples of Aoaz. He died in battle with the servant and helped force it to withdraw. He lived long after Dardan, but he did not outlive the Fourth Age.

plate.subject: Horos standing with the blue sword, from the established description (A6)

paragraphs.text: Horos is a Great Spirit, lord of the Castle of Yeldenne in the Cold Lands and guardian of Glo. He is an enormous knight in yellow-green armour, with strange branching spikes upon his helm, glowing blue eyes and a blue sword of magic. He keeps his throne in a dark hall, and deep halls lie beneath his castle.

Glo shows as a green jewel before his throne: a crystal of old and holy power, said to hold part of the power of Glernaen, the New God of Power and Wisdom. Within his castle Horos is far stronger than anywhere else.

Horos died when an intruder came to his castle for Glo. Then the truth of the crystal was known: Glo was Horos’s own heart, and he had carried his own strength as a Great Spirit together with the power entrusted to him by a god. His body turned to dust. What became of his spirit is not known.

A crowned intruder from the south came to Yeldenne for Glo. Horos challenged him and warned him to leave, and he refused. In their struggle Horos seized him, but the intruder vanished from his grasp, appeared behind him and stabbed him in the back of the neck.

Then the Man from the Ice arrived, wounded the intruder and forced him to flee. Dying, Horos gave Glo and his blue sword to the Man from the Ice. He drew out his own crystal heart with his hands, and he crumbled to dust.
The intruder was Afrit. Before they fought, Horos named him for what he was, the brother of Eindil.
When an intruder came to the castle for Glo, Horos held his hall and drove him out. Glo still lies before his throne.

plate.subject: an old wizard with a lantern among standing stones

paragraphs.text: Varner is a wise wizard of the Magical Lands, a Lesser Spirit in the form of an old man. Through the long Third Age he helped the elves and the resistance of men withstand Elzon’s necromancy, for he can undo the curse that binds the risen dead. His wisdom has stayed influential for centuries since.

A small purple servant of unknown origin, Golbran, goes with him. For all his fame Varner is a Lesser Spirit, and one practitioner among many traditions of magic. Bastian, a living human wizard famous in the Middle Lands, is of his time.

In the War of the Last Crowns Varner came to Aenor on a dragon with the Man from the Ice and Golbran. He shielded the living armies from the death-magic of Zol and spent his last strength to open a way for them to survive. He died when Zol’s forces threatened to overwhelm the defenders, and the time he won them was essential to all that followed.

plate.subject: a small purple humanoid figure at a wizard's side

paragraphs.text: Golbran is the small, purple, humanoid servant and companion of the wizard Varner. His kind and his origin are unknown. He stood with Varner against Elzon in the Third Age and has lived on into the Fourth.
Small as he is, Golbran is a creature of magic. He does not age, though he can be slain.
Golbran died at the end of the Fourth Age. He gave the last of his life and magic to save the one he fought beside, at the price of his own.

In the royal palace Golbran used his magic to remove the Necklace of the Abyss from Afrit, leaving the god-king mortal and vulnerable. After Eindil killed Afrit, Golbran gave Eindil his last remaining life and magic and so saved him.

plate.subject: a ranger drawing a bow at a forest edge

paragraphs.text: Alleria is a celebrated ranger and archer of Selen, in the Middle Lands. No chronicle tells where she learned her craft, nor of her family or her age.

When the stranger’s warnings came to the Middle Lands and most of Aenor denounced him, Alleria looked into the rumours about him. She led a hidden band loyal to the old royal line, and it sheltered the stranger.
After Afrit threw the stranger from the cliff, Alleria and her band brought him up out of the ravine alive.

In the royal palace Alleria shot Afrit in the eye. In that moment Eindil cut off one of Afrit’s fingers and took a ring, and Alleria went on helping him disable the enchanted artifacts that kept Afrit’s overwhelming strength.

plate.subject: a storm-shrouded vast shadow over red desert, no clear face

paragraphs.text: Volgan is a Great Spirit and the principal dark lord of Aoaz. He has existed for immense ages, and his domain is the Ember Lands. His armies include demons, orcs, goblins, monsters, necromantic hosts and other spirits. The independent Dark Lands are not his subjects by right.

The oldest elves say that Volgan was once the servant of a New God, and that he overcame that god and founded his own dominion by means no chronicle tells. The chronicles of men do not. Which god it was, and what became of it, is not known.

In the First Age Volgan invaded Mirolon and advanced to Aenor’s capital. King Edran’s Grand Alliance defeated him at Dardan, where other spirits stripped his active power and banished him to the Void. In the Second Age Elzon restored his soul or presence from the Void. Through the long Third Age Volgan was too weak to leave the Ember Lands, and he gave his orders to Elzon, who ruled Aenor in his name.
Volgan is a wizard of green magic and not human in form. He is a purple cloak filled with darkness, in which only his glowing green eyes can be seen, and his crown floats above the dark.
Recovered at last, Volgan marched north from the Ember Lands with an army greater than any Aoaz had seen.
The Man from the Ice pierced Volgan with the divine sword of Horos, and Volgan’s manifested body burst apart. His army lost much of its unnatural order. Whether his spirit survives is not known.

entries.title: Elzon, the Great Necromancer
entries.subtitle: Second and Third Ages · Great Spirit

plate.subject: a pale robed shape among risen dead, face in shadow

paragraphs.text: Elzon was a Great Spirit, the Great Necromancer, and the devoted servant of Volgan. His home was Nazerun, the old name of Nezer, in the Ember Lands. No chronicle tells where he learned necromancy, or what he was before he served Volgan.

After Volgan was defeated at Dardan and banished to the Void, Elzon gathered his remaining forces in the Ember Lands. He had prepared the defence, and he threw back the Grand Alliance when it tried to invade. Many of the attackers died, elves among them, and the invasion failed. The victorious king of that alliance was Edran.

Through the Second Age Elzon directed raids and built networks to keep Aenor from rising again. He made alliances with orcs, goblins, corrupt rulers, monsters and other dark powers, without ruling them all. At last he freed Volgan from the Void and returned his soul to Aoaz. Volgan came back weak and granted Elzon greater freedom.

Elzon also borrowed old magic tied to Zol, the first stirring of that Old God in the known history of men; how he obtained it, and whether Zol willed it, is not known. Then he took the field openly and raised the dead, turning men slain while resisting him into his own soldiers. Aenor’s allies were divided or corrupted, and in the Second Age year 2133 Elzon conquered Aenor and set up his Order. So began the Third Age.

sources.section: Third Age rule and final death

paragraphs.text: In the Third Age Elzon ruled Aenor in fact, still obeying Volgan. His risen host faded with time, and his own power ran down in Aenor, whose magic did not renew him as the Ember Lands did. He sought the power to make Aenor a land that would sustain him. Men went on resisting, and the Magical Lands held free with the help of Varner, a Lesser Spirit able to lift the curse of the dead, and his purple servant Golbran.

sources.section: Third Age rule and final death
Third Age limitations and permanent death

paragraphs.text: Elzon’s rule ended in his literal and permanent death. In the Last Tithe the resistance of men and Varner broke the spells that upheld him, and Elzon overdrew the death-magic he had borrowed from Zol, so that his spirit was consumed entirely. In that ruin the Deliverer shielded the people.
paragraphs.note: the Last Tithe and the manner of his death are proposed; his permanent death is established

sources.section: Third Age rule and final death
Third Age limitations and permanent death

entries.title: Roka of the Abyss
entries.subtitle: Ember Lands · Folk of the Abyss

plate.subject: a rhinoceros-headed giant in a deep chasm

paragraphs.text: Roka belongs to the Abyss in the Ember Lands, and the powerful Necklace of the Abyss is bound up with his name. He is one of a people of large, rhinoceros-headed humanoids who come from the Abyss. Their name, their history and the order of their society are not known.
Why the necklace holds such extreme power, and whether Roka himself guarded it, no chronicle tells. Nor is Roka’s own fate known.

Agon was a demon active in the Second Age, linked with the Nether in the south of the Ember Lands. In his time other demons grew ever more active, and portals and raids threatened Aenor and other peoples.

Agon’s order among folk and spirits, his rank in war, his allegiance and his history are not known. Nor is it known how he stood with the King of Demons. That king holds his seat in the Nether, but no chronicle says that Agon was he.

entries.title: The King of Demons
entries.subtitle: All Ages · Lord of the Nether

paragraphs.text: A King of Demons holds his seat in the southern Nether of the Ember Lands. No chronicle gives his name. His pacts bind the living; the souls of the dead remain Zol’s.

His powers and his kind of demon are not known, nor how he stands with Volgan, with Elzon or with Agon. His title makes him a ruler within the society of demons. It does not make every demon his subject, nor all who are born in the Nether, nor the demons who serve other powers.

plate.subject: a crowned ranger before a rebuilt gate

paragraphs.text: Harion of Selen was the first king of the restored Aenor, crowned after the permanent death of Elzon at the end of the Third Age. He came of a side branch of Aen’s royal line and earned his place through many years of resistance and organising. His right to rule rested on both his descent and his service.
Harion brought peace through rebuilding, law, the fair storage of grain, sensible defence and diplomacy. He welcomed the Deliverer’s houses of relief, because they plainly helped the people.
The Fourth Age that followed has lasted more than a thousand years, ruled by successive kings and royal generations. Harion himself did not live or reign through all of it.

entries.title: Merovan of the Seals
entries.subtitle: Fourth Age · Keeper of the Seals of Aenor

paragraphs.text: Merovan is Keeper of the Seals of Aenor, a long-serving courtier of the royal government. He holds the ordinary authority of a high councillor and has long advised the Golden King.

Merovan sits on Afrit’s Hidden Council. Beside his office he commands hidden agents who report to Afrit. In him the long decades of a compromised government, which led toward the open seizure of the crown, took a human face.
When the Deliverer left Parim for the Cold Lands, Merovan was left to hold the seals and to administer Aenor in his place.

Sevrin is the master thief whom Afrit sent into the Abyss of the Ember Lands to obtain Roka’s Necklace of the Abyss. In 4A 1611 he succeeded. Afrit had promised him eternal life, and he kept the promise through the power of the necklace.
paragraphs.note: the name Sevrin and the year 4A 1611 are proposed; the thief, the mission and the eternal life are established

paragraphs.text: Sevrin does not age, but he can be wounded and he can be trapped. His long life is bound to Afrit’s power. He understands the necklace better than any sorcerer of a court.
Whether Sevrin’s life outlasted Afrit’s death, no chronicle tells.

entries.title: The Free Banners of Dardan
entries.subtitle: First Age · Captains of the Alliance

paragraphs.text: Many captains came to King Edran’s Grand Alliance from free peoples who owed Aenor nothing, and the Charter of the Free Banners kept their freedom. Five of them stand out in the histories of Dardan.

sources.section: Proposed characters of the First Age

paragraphs.text: Sirael was the elected war-speaker of the elves of the Magical Forest. Those elves choose their own leaders, and Sirael spoke for a free people, never as a crowned ruler beside the hereditary kings of the other elves.

sources.section: Proposed characters of the First Age

paragraphs.text: Taryn, a commander of the West Lands, demanded guarantees for the West before aiding the kingdom that had taken the western lands as its own. Senra of the Pupor Isles, a captain of the island fleets, carried the alliance’s supplies by sea and moved its troops across far waters.

sources.section: Proposed characters of the First Age

paragraphs.text: Brunek of the Stone Roads, a dwarven engineer of war, held the crossings at Dardan beside the giants. Rovek of Dondor, a free lord of the Dark Lands, marched against Volgan and showed that the Dark Lands had never stood united behind him. Not all of Dondor followed Rovek.

sources.section: Proposed characters of the First Age

paragraphs.text: Two Great Spirits stood with the Grand Alliance against Volgan. Ithren of the Threshold, a spirit of boundaries, helped work Volgan’s banishment at Dardan and was bound into the ward that held him. It was a working of spirits, not of the gods.

sources.section: Proposed characters of the First Age

paragraphs.text: Maerul of the Deep Stone fought the Damned Spirits and helped seal the ruptures that opened beneath the earth.

sources.section: Proposed characters of the First Age

paragraphs.text: Great Spirits are immortal, yet they can be bound or shattered. In the Second Age Ithren’s ward failed, and through its failing Elzon recovered the banished Volgan.
Vareth the Pale commanded the corrupted elves who marched in Volgan’s host in the First Age.

sources.section: Proposed characters of the First Age

paragraphs.text: Not every elf stood with the Grand Alliance. Vareth’s banners showed how far corruption had reached among the elf peoples, and how divided their loyalties had become.

sources.section: Proposed characters of the First Age

paragraphs.text: While Elzon’s war spread through the Second Age, captains of several peoples kept faith with Aenor. The histories remember three.

Avarin of Lerendor’s North served the North Lands as envoy and later as commander. She tried to bring aid to Aenor while defending her own kingdom, and her impossible place showed why the Grand Alliance could not simply be raised again.

Seron of Selen, a commander of men, guarded the rebuilding of the provinces and their roads of supply. His campaigns steadied whole districts for a time, but he lost men faster than they could be replaced. He and Avarin never agreed whether force of arms could save the kingdom. No chronicle tells how Seron’s war ended.

Tavriel of the Magical Forest, an elven healer and keeper of wards, went on helping men despite the resentment many elves bore Aenor. Her opponents among the elves argued for closing the borders, and she sheltered the very refugees her own people feared.

entries.title: Arelon, Keeper of the Last Seal
entries.subtitle: Second Age · Royal Archivist

paragraphs.text: Arelon was a royal archivist of Aenor. When Elzon conquered the kingdom at the close of the Second Age, Arelon escaped with fragments of the lineages of Aen and with the ancient law of succession.
Aenor’s fall began the Third Age under Elzon’s Order. No chronicle names the royal capital of that day or its last free king, nor tells what became of the royal line.
Arelon believed that saving the memory of Aenor might matter even if its walls could not be saved. What became of his archive, no chronicle tells.

entries.title: Kusven
entries.subtitle: Fourth Age · Legend of the North

paragraphs.text: The winter tales of the north tell of Kusven, the servant of Zol, the Old God of Death. His name is a Leren word meaning “the grave-wind”, and the sea north of Zol’s Mistake is called Kusmeel, “the grave-sea”. The Leren fishers who winter on the black isles keep the tale among the oldest customs owed to the Old God.

The shore folk and the sailors say that Kusven is Zol’s most loyal servant, and that he is not Zol himself but a being of his own. They say that he dwells on Šodolôro in Zol’s Mistake, that he feeds on souls, and that he covets all of Aoaz. All who tell of him fear him.
What Kusven truly is, no chronicle tells. It is not known whether he rules the Mistake or its seat Furviatlon, nor how his hunger for souls stands beside Zol’s claim on the souls of the dead.
In the War of the Last Crowns Kusven came forth out of the black north and took the field. Zol himself did not appear; his servant carried the Old God’s power onto the field.
Kusven broke the blue sword of Horos, but the Man from the Ice wounded him with a shard of the blade, which still bore divine magic.
Kusven withdrew into the north. He was not destroyed. What the war cost him, no chronicle tells.
Lorien of the Gala and ancient spirits died opposing him, and their stand forced him back.
